newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland back on brink after soldier killed.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland back on brink after soldier killed.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major vowed on Thursday there would be no hiding place for the suspected IRA gunman who killed a British soldier and pushed Northern Ireland back to the brink of war.
The soldier was manning a checkpoint outside the southern village of Bessbrook and talking to a woman in a car when he was hit by a shot from a high velocity rifle on Wednesday night.

Bessbrook is the British army's helicopter base for patrols in the so-called "bandit country" of south Armagh where IRA snipers killed seven people before calling a ceasefire in September 1994 which they ended on February 9 last year.

The woman was slightly injured but the soldier was pronounced dead minutes later, the first fatality of the Northern Ireland conflict of 1997 and the first to die of a gunshot wound since before the IRA truce.
Lance Bombardier Stephen Restorick was 23.
"There was a young man smiling at me and then the next minute he was on the ground. It was just so sad -- it shouldn't happen," eyewitness Lorraine McElroy told GMTV television.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility but the British and Irish governmenents quickly blamed the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which has fought a 28-year war to oust Britain and reunite the province with Ireland.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said: "The IRA campaign is anti-Irish and contrary to the interests of all in Ireland."
Major said he presumed the soldier was another victim of the "murderous efforts" of the IRA and asked:
"How many more victims must there be before the evil men responsible recognise the utter futility of their terrorism?

"Let me make two promises ... there will be no hiding place for the culprits -- none at all -- and I will not be deflected from the real search for a lasting settlement and peace in Northern Ireland."
The killing, the first since the IRA bombed a British army base last October killing one soldier and injuring 30, put intense strain on a ceasefire by their Protestant Loyalist foes.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew urged them to resist the temptation to hit back.
"Don't lower yourselves to the standards, the level, of the people who have done this," he implored on BBC radio.
Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, have officially stuck by an October 1994 ceasefire but have warned that if the IRA kills they will go back on the warpath.
They killed hundreds from the Catholic community, from which the IRA draws support, to avenge IRA attacks in a conflict which has killed a total of 3,200 including hundreds of IRA victims.
Security sources believe the IRA is trying to cause mayhem in Northern Ireland so that whoever wins British elections due by May 22 has to act decisively to get Sinn Fein to the table.

But neither Major, nor his likely successor, Labour leader Tony Blair, have shown signs on backing down on demands that the IRA end its war for good to earn a right to negotiate with Protestant leaders who want to stay British.
Mayhew vowed the government would act in the interests of the peace process and not seek to score points with Ulster Unionists and thereby shore up its own standing in parliament.
To suggest Major would seek votes on the back on the peace process was to underestimate the prime minister, he said.
Britain has 18,000 troops in Northern Ireland who have been on high alert since the IRA ended a 17-month truce one year ago accusing Britain of blocking Sinn Fein's path to the talks.
